body_markdown:
SUMMARY


**Automatically blurring faces and license plates before data enters a storage pipeline is a practical way to handle personally identifiable information in computer vision deployments, following the same approach used by Google Maps Street View. This tutorial covers collecting face and license plate datasets from Roboflow Universe, training a detection model, and using the Roboflow API to run inference and then apply OpenCV blur or pixelation to each detected region of interest. The result is an anonymization step that can be inserted into any image or video pipeline without changing downstream processing.**


**Quote of the day:**
*“Keep calm and carry on.”* -Winston Churchill


Computer vision applications can be used in a variety of settings and sometimes information captured in your dataset might not be information you want to be responsible for having such as personally identifiable information, banking information, or any other sensitive data.


In these instances, you can ensure the data is anonymized by blurring, pixelating, or fogging any specific data before it enters your database. This post will show you how to do this using computer vision.


### What to expect from this blog post?


1. How to train models to detect faces and license plates from a given image.
2. Using the[Roboflow API (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/deployment/legacy/legacy-serverless?ref=blog.roboflow.com) **** to run the trained model on your custom images.
3. Automatically censor detected[faces (opens in a new tab)](https://universe.roboflow.com/roboflow-qsmu6/face-blur-nsz4h?ref=blog.roboflow.com) and[license plates](https://app.roboflow.com/roboflow-qsmu6/license-plate-riofh/1https://universe.roboflow.com/roboflow-qsmu6/license-plate-riofh/dataset/1?ref=blog.roboflow.com) to anonymize data captured in computer vision projects.


### What is Fogging or Blurring in Computer Vision?


Fogging, also known as blurring, is used for censorship or privacy in which a visual area of any image, video, or livestream is blurred to obscure the data captured.


Example of face blurring or fogging with computer visionExample of license plate fogging


Pixelization ****** is also a form of fogging. This technique is used widely across industries from street mapping to news reporting to social media.


### Example: Face Blurring Used in Google Maps


When Street View imagery is published to Google Maps, Google employs censoring faces to protect individuals’ privacy.


Google Maps blurring faces preserving privacy


### Steps Involved for Blurring Faces with Computer Vision


Just 3 simple steps:


- Step 1: Collect data
- Step 2: Train a model
- Step 3: Use the Roboflow API to deploy the model


### Collect Data of Faces for Model Training


Luckily, we have[Roboflow Universe (opens in a new tab)](https://universe.roboflow.com/?ref=blog.roboflow.com) which is home to the world's largest collection of annotated and ready to use datasets related to various industries such as[self-driving cars (opens in a new tab)](https://universe.roboflow.com/browse/self-driving?ref=blog.roboflow.com) and[agriculture (opens in a new tab)](https://universe.roboflow.com/browse/agriculture?ref=blog.roboflow.com) , to[manufacturing (opens in a new tab)](https://universe.roboflow.com/browse/manufacturing?ref=blog.roboflow.com) and[gaming (opens in a new tab)](https://universe.roboflow.com/browse/gaming?ref=blog.roboflow.com) that are open source and free to use. *Tip: Search using the keyword 'faces' or 'license plates' and we are ready to go*


Visual tutorial on how to collect data using Roboflow Universe


In addition to downloading the datasets, you can also[clone data from Roboflow Universe (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/datasets/create-and-upload/adding-data/roboflow-universe#clone-images-to-your-roboflow-project) directly to a project in your Roboflow account.


If you need additional data beyond what is provided in Universe, you can[upload Youtube videos as training data (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/datasets/create-and-upload/adding-data#uploading-youtube-videos) or[upload your own data (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/datasets/create-and-upload/adding-data?ref=blog.roboflow.com) . Then you'll use[Roboflow Annotate](https://roboflow.com/annotate?ref=blog.roboflow.com) to label the data for model training.


### Train a Face Detection Model


We then upload our downloaded image dataset to the[Roboflow app](https://app.roboflow.com/?ref=blog.roboflow.com) to train our model to detect faces. This process can be done for any data you want to obfuscate and anonymize such as[license plates (opens in a new tab)](https://universe.roboflow.com/carplates2/licenseplate_v2?ref=blog.roboflow.com) and[identification cards (opens in a new tab)](https://universe.roboflow.com/nitrille-nrade/docs-nmmol/browse?queryText=&pageSize=50&startingIndex=0&browseQuery=true&ref=blog.roboflow.com) .


Steps to train a face blurring model using Roboflow


After uploading your dataset,[properly labeling the data](https://roboflow.com/blog/tips-for-how-to-label-images) , adding[augmentations](https://roboflow.com/blog/boosting-image-detection-performance-with-data-augmentation) , and generating the dataset, you can[train a computer vision model with one-click using Roboflow Train](https://roboflow.com/train?ref=blog.roboflow.com) .


Below are the results after training the model using the[Accurate model (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/models) ** in Roboflow.


One-click training results using Roboflow


Along with model performance data, we also have access to visualizations for the training and validation curves.


Model training visualizations


### Using the Computer Vision Model to Censor the Region of Interest (ROI)


After successfully training the model, go to the[Deploy page (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/deployment) and use the API script provided to censor the images.


Roboflow deployment API


After training, call your model from Python with the Roboflow inference SDK, then use[supervision (opens in a new tab)](https://github.com/roboflow/supervision?ref=blog.roboflow.com) , Roboflow's open source computer vision library, to blur or pixelate every detected face. Install both packages:


Shell


```text
pip   install   inference-sdk   supervision
```


Run the model on an image and convert the response into a supervision` Detections` object. Replace` MODEL_ID` with your project ID and version from your model's[Deploy page (opens in a new tab)](https://docs.roboflow.com/deployment) , and add your Roboflow API key.


Python


```text
import   cv2
import   supervision   as   sv
from   inference_sdk   import   InferenceHTTPClient


client   =   InferenceHTTPClient(
api_url  =  "https://serverless.roboflow.com"  ,
api_key  =  "YOUR_ROBOFLOW_API_KEY"  ,
)
MODEL_ID   =   "your-project/1"    # your face (or license plate) model ID and version


image   =   cv2.imread(  "people.jpg"  )
result   =   client.infer(image,   model_id  =  MODEL_ID  )
detections   =   sv.Detections.from_inference(result)
detections   =   detections[detections.confidence   >   0.4  ]
```


The model returns one prediction per face with the box center, width, height, class, and confidence:


Sample JSON output from the model


After the prediction, extract the region of interest (ROI):


Python


```text
roi   =   sv.crop_image(  image  =  image,   xyxy  =  detections.xyxy[  0  ])
```


To blur every face, use` BlurAnnotator` . A larger` kernel_size` gives a stronger blur; 35 hides facial features without overdoing it.


Python


```text
blur_annotator   =   sv.BlurAnnotator(  kernel_size  =  35  )
blurred   =   blur_annotator.annotate(  scene  =  image.copy(),   detections  =  detections)
cv2.imwrite(  "blurred.jpg"  , blurred)
```


To pixelate instead, use` PixelateAnnotator` . A larger` pixel_size` gives bigger blocks.


Python


```text
pixelate_annotator   =   sv.PixelateAnnotator(  pixel_size  =  12  )
pixelated   =   pixelate_annotator.annotate(  scene  =  image.copy(),   detections  =  detections)
cv2.imwrite(  "pixelated.jpg"  , pixelated)
```


Example usage of protecting children's privacy


Both annotators cover every face the model finds, so group photos and crowded scenes are handled in one call.


### Blur Faces in Video


The same annotator works frame by frame.` sv.process_video` reads a video, runs your callback on each frame, and writes the anonymized result:


Python


```text
def   callback  (frame, index):
result   =   client.infer(frame,   model_id  =  MODEL_ID  )
detections   =   sv.Detections.from_inference(result)
detections   =   detections[detections.confidence   >   0.4  ]
return   blur_annotator.annotate(  scene  =  frame.copy(),   detections  =  detections)


sv.process_video(  source_path  =  "input.mp4"  ,   target_path  =  "blurred.mp4"  ,   callback  =  callback)
```
